name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q01 - Three-statement evaluation on 3d transition elements

questiontext.text:
Consider the following three statements regarding the \(3d\) series elements:

I. Scandium (\(Z = 21\)) does not exhibit variable oxidation states and shows only the \(+3\) oxidation state.

II. Zinc (\(Z = 30\)) is regarded as a transition metal because it is the end member of the \(3d\) series.

III. Manganese (\(Z = 25\)) exhibits the largest number of oxidation states (from \(+2\) to \(+7\)) in the \(3d\) series.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Transition elements are defined by IUPAC as metals with an incomplete \(d\) subshell in their neutral atom or common ions. Their variable oxidation states depend on the availability of both \(ns\) and unpaired \((n-1)d\) electrons.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Claim
The claim regarding scandium is correct: \(\mathrm{Sc}\) (\([\mathrm{Ar}]3d^14s^2\)) loses all three valence electrons to form \(\mathrm{Sc^{3+}}\) and does not exhibit variable oxidation states. The claim regarding zinc is incorrect: \(\mathrm{Zn}\) has a completely filled \(3d^{10}\) configuration in both its neutral ground state and its \(+2\) oxidation state (\(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\)), so it is not regarded as a transition metal. The claim regarding manganese is correct: lying in the middle of the \(3d\) series with a \(3d^54s^2\) configuration, \(\mathrm{Mn}\) exhibits all oxidation states from \(+2\) to \(+7\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Only the claims regarding scandium and manganese are correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q02 - Three-statement evaluation on interstitial compounds, Group 6 stability, and complexes

questiontext.text:
Consider the following three statements regarding transition metals and their compounds:

I. Interstitial compounds of transition metals have higher melting points than pure metals and retain metallic conductivity.

II. In Group 6, \(\mathrm{Mo(VI)}\) and \(\mathrm{W(VI)}\) are more stable than \(\mathrm{Cr(VI)}\), making dichromate in acidic medium a strong oxidising agent whereas \(\mathrm{MoO_3}\) and \(\mathrm{WO_3}\) are not.

III. Transition metals form a large number of complex compounds due to their comparatively smaller ionic sizes, high ionic charges, and availability of \(d\) orbitals.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Transition metals exhibit characteristic properties including interstitial compound formation, group-wise stability trends in higher oxidation states, and coordination complex formation.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Claim
The claim on interstitial compounds is correct: trapping small atoms like \(\mathrm{H}\), \(\mathrm{C}\), or \(\mathrm{N}\) in metal crystal lattices yields hard, chemically inert materials with higher melting points than pure metals that still retain metallic conductivity. The claim on Group 6 oxidation states is also correct: unlike \(p\)-block groups, heavier \(d\)-block members (\(\mathrm{Mo(VI)}\) and \(\mathrm{W(VI)}\)) are more stable in higher oxidation states than \(\mathrm{Cr(VI)}\), so \(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}}\) is a strong oxidant in acid while \(\mathrm{MoO_3}\) and \(\mathrm{WO_3}\) are not. The claim on complex formation is also correct: small ionic size, high charge, and vacant \(d\) orbitals enable transition metal ions to bind ligands readily.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
All three claims are factually correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q03 - Three-statement evaluation on lanthanoids and actinoids

questiontext.text:
Consider the following three statements regarding the inner transition (\(f\)-block) elements:

I. In aqueous solution, \(\mathrm{Ce^{4+}}\) (\(4f^0\)) acts as a strong reducing agent while \(\mathrm{Eu^{2+}}\) (\(4f^7\)) acts as a strong oxidising agent.

II. Actinoids exhibit a wider range of oxidation states than lanthanoids because the \(5f\), \(6d\), and \(7s\) levels in actinoids are of comparable energies.

III. The actinoid contraction is greater from element to element than the lanthanoid contraction because \(5f\) electrons provide poorer shielding than \(4f\) electrons.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In lanthanoids, \(+3\) is the most stable oxidation state, so \(+2\) and \(+4\) ions tend to revert to \(+3\). In actinoids, orbital energy comparability and poor \(5f\) shielding govern oxidation states and ionic size trends.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Claim
The claim regarding \(\mathrm{Ce^{4+}}\) and \(\mathrm{Eu^{2+}}\) is incorrect: \(\mathrm{Ce^{4+}}\) reverts to \(\mathrm{Ce^{3+}}\) by gaining an electron and is therefore a strong oxidant (\(E^\circ = +1.74\,\mathrm{V}\)), whereas \(\mathrm{Eu^{2+}}\) reverts to \(\mathrm{Eu^{3+}}\) by losing an electron and is a strong reducing agent. The claim regarding oxidation state range is correct: the comparable energies of \(5f\), \(6d\), and \(7s\) orbitals allow actinoids to display a much wider range of oxidation states (up to \(+7\)). The claim regarding contraction is also correct: \(5f\) electrons shield the nuclear charge even more poorly than \(4f\) electrons, resulting in a greater element-to-element contraction across the actinoid series.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Only the claims regarding the wider range of actinoid oxidation states and the greater actinoid contraction are correct.
